title: An Interview with Drew and Megan Dickerson: Marriage, Family, and the Intellectual Life
author: Nadya Williams
summary: Nadya Williams interviews Drew and Megan Dickerson, a married couple who are both finishing theology PhDs at Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary while raising four school-aged children. The piece is the third in a Mere Orthodoxy series asking how the intellectual life works in households where both spouses are scholars, since writers and thinkers must also eat, do laundry and keep children alive. Each describes an unplanned path: Megan was shaped by an honors liberal arts programme and a circle of homeschooling mothers who read theology and fiction together, while Drew moved from student ministry into library work and teaching. They explain how reading together is part of their marriage, how dinner-table talk ranges from the incarnation to football, and how their children grow up surrounded by books while still playing sports and watching more YouTube than Megan would like. They are candid about the pile of laundry on the couch, a hospital stay that stalled their dissertations, and the way different seasons of motherhood change what intellectual work is possible. Their shared hope is to keep one foot in the church and one in the academy, teaching and forming students.
points: The intellectual life in a family is a matter of seasons, and Megan notes that she kept reading while drowning in toddlers even though it was not the season for a PhD.
Reading together and talking about ideas is a central, deliberate practice in the Dickersons' marriage and a shared interest that drew them together.
Family culture centred on books and faith can coexist with sports, video games and ordinary mess, since the intellectual life is not the whole personality of anyone in the home.
Small, relational forms of teaching, such as meeting one-on-one with younger women to read the Bible, count as genuine intellectual and pastoral work during demanding family seasons.

Practical constraints such as laundry, driving kids to practice and illness are the real test of any scholarly vocation, and the couple handle them by stepping through the doors that open rather than forcing a plan.
quotes: Writers and other intellectuals are people too—they too must eat, do laundry, keep children alive, perhaps even vacuum on occasion. We all are bodies, as well as minds and souls.
I’ve always liked to read and think and ask questions and that has usually gotten me in trouble or been viewed with suspicion.

But when I got to college, I felt God calling me to use my gifts, including my mind, to serve the church. At the time, I had no idea what that looked like, but I went to seminary and had an amazing experience getting to study ancient languages, church history, and theology.

I get to tell them that there are seasons, and God wants you to use your gifts, including your academic gets, for the church, but that we don’t have to feel the pressure to lean into all of these gifts at the same time.

Drew and I knew we wanted to get married, because we like to think and talk about ideas, because we like to read. Not that we would have thought about this as an intellectual life. But reading together and talking about what we’re reading is a big part of our marriage.
We challenge our kids to read good books, think well, and ask good questions. But it’s fun to see how that plays out in each of their lives.
But I think our family culture is centered on reading and loving Jesus, and that’s evident in the lives of our kids.
Over time, we’ve learned to pursue excellence in whatever we do and step through the doors that God opens for us.
